guide.title: Chelsea, Manhattan: Freight Rails Into Gallery Row
guide.intro: Chelsea takes its name from a 1750 country estate that retired British Major Thomas Clarke named after London's Royal Hospital Chelsea. Clement Clarke Moore, credited with writing 'A Visit From St. Nicholas,' inherited the estate, donated his apple orchard to the General Theological Seminary in 1827, and laid out the rest as residential lots under covenants barring commercial use. The 1847 Hudson River Railroad undid that plan: freight tracks along the waterfront brought distilleries, gas works, and piers worked largely by Irish immigrants, and West 23rd Street grew into a theater district after Pike's Opera House opened in 1868. The 1883 Hotel Chelsea rose amid that district and became one of New York's most storied artists' residences. Beginning in the late 1990s, galleries priced out of SoHo turned West Chelsea into the city's contemporary-art hub, joining a neighborhood with a substantial LGBTQ community since the mid-1980s.

sections.heading: From Freight Line to Gallery District
sections.body: The elevated freight viaduct now known as the High Line ran its first train in 1933, carrying coal, dairy, and beef directly into Chelsea's warehouses; its last train, hauling frozen turkeys, ran in 1980. After decades of disuse it reopened as a public park in phases starting June 8, 2009, drawing about eight million visitors a year by 2019 and helping pull West Chelsea's more than 200 art galleries into one of the city's densest concentrations of contemporary art. The Hotel Chelsea, built 1883–1885 on West 23rd Street, predates all of it — Dylan Thomas was staying there in 1953 when he was taken to St. Vincent's Hospital, where he died.

sections.heading: Getting there by subway
sections.body: Chelsea is ringed by three north-south trunk lines: A/C/E on Eighth Avenue (14 St and 23 St–8 Av), 1/2/3 on Seventh Avenue (14 St, 18 St, and 23 St), and F/M on Sixth Avenue, plus the L train's Manhattan terminus at 14 St/8 Av and the 7 at 34 St–Hudson Yards on the neighborhood's northern edge. For the gallery district and the High Line, 23 St–8 Av (C/E) is the closest stop.

sections.heading: Chelsea Market and the Piers
sections.body: Chelsea Market, in a former Nabisco factory at 75 Ninth Avenue, is an indoor food hall with vendors including Buddakan and Mokbar; the concourse is open daily 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. On the waterfront, Chelsea Piers occupies the historic Hudson River piers with a marina, ice rink, and driving range, roughly 30 years into its run since opening in 1995. Just south, the High Line's Gansevoort Street terminus and the Whitney Museum of American Art sit over the Meatpacking District line, and Little Island's tulip-shaped piers rise from the river a few blocks further down.

faq.question: How do I get to Chelsea by subway?
faq.answer: A/C/E on Eighth Avenue and 1/2/3 on Seventh Avenue both stop at 14th and 23rd Streets, with F/M on Sixth Avenue and the L terminating at 14 St/8 Av. For the galleries and the High Line, get off at 23 St–8 Av (C/E).

faq.question: Where did Chelsea get its name?
faq.answer: From a 1750 country estate that British Major Thomas Clarke named after London's Royal Hospital Chelsea; his descendant Clement Clarke Moore later developed the land into residential lots.

faq.question: Is the Hotel Chelsea open to visit?
faq.answer: It operates as a hotel again, with three in-house restaurants — El Quijote, Café Chelsea, and Teruko — after reopening in 2022 following renovation. Non-guests can visit the restaurants and lobby.

faq.question: Can I still see the Rubin Museum's collection in Chelsea?
faq.answer: No — the Rubin's West 17th Street building is no longer open to visitors; the museum now operates through traveling exhibitions and partner institutions rather than a Chelsea location.

faq.question: Is the High Line free?
faq.answer: Yes. The 1.45-mile elevated park is free and open daily, with wheelchair-accessible entrances at Gansevoort, 14th, 16th, 23rd, and 30th Streets.

places.name: Chelsea Market
places.summary: An indoor food hall and shopping concourse with vendors including Lobster Place, Amy's Bread, and Mokbar; open daily 7 a.m. to 10 p.m.

places.name: The Joyce Theater
places.summary: A dance-dedicated theater — 'New York's Home for Dance' — whose auditorium is formally named the Tino & Rajika Puri Auditorium, running a 40-45 week annual season.

places.name: Chelsea Piers
places.address: Piers 59-61, Hudson River between 17th and 23rd Streets (entrance at 23rd St/West Side Highway), New York, NY
places.summary: A sports and entertainment complex on the historic Hudson River piers, open since August 1995, with Sky Rink ice skating, a golf club and driving range, fitness clubs, and a marina.

places.name: Cookshop
places.summary: A restaurant at 156 Tenth Avenue, across from the High Line's 23rd Street stretch. By its own account its menus change frequently, based on the freshest ingredients available in the market and from purveyors in the Northeast.

places.name: Buddakan
places.summary: The New York branch of Stephen Starr's Pan-Asian chain, inside Chelsea Market at 75 Ninth Avenue; the first Buddakan opened in Philadelphia in 1998, at 325 Chestnut Street. The menu is built to share — dim sum, noodle soups, seafood and whole Peking duck. A Meatpacking District neighborhood site describes it as a 260-seat modern Chinese restaurant.

places.name: Billy's Bakery (Chelsea)
places.address: 184 Ninth Avenue (at 21st St), New York, NY
places.summary: A bakery that dates its own beginnings to 2003 and 'two friends from business school,' without naming them or saying which storefront came first. It sells cakes, cupcakes, cookies, cheesecakes, pies, bars and breakfast items, and its Chelsea storefront is one of three Manhattan locations.

places.name: Mokbar (Chelsea Market)
places.address: Inside Chelsea Market, 75 9th Avenue, New York, NY 10011
places.summary: A Korean kitchen inside Chelsea Market specializing in Korean street-food noodles and 'Anju,' shareable small plates, with the everyday food culture of Korea given as its inspiration. Chef Esther Choi is associated with it. Beyond Chelsea Market it has locations in Midtown, on Lexington Avenue, and in Brooklyn at 212 Flatbush Avenue near Barclays Center.

places.name: Hotel Chelsea
places.summary: The landmark 1883-1885 artists' hotel where Dylan Thomas spent his final days before his death at St. Vincent's Hospital; reopened as a hotel in 2022 with in-house restaurants El Quijote, Café Chelsea, and Teruko.

photos.title: Hotel Chelsea
photos.description: The neon sign and facade of the Hotel Chelsea at night.
photos.author: Summermother

places.name: The Maritime Hotel
places.summary: A hotel that opened in 2003 with 121 rooms and 5 suites decorated on a nautical theme, in the West 16th Street building nicknamed the 'pizza box,' which has porthole-style window openings. It participates in the Lifestyle Preferred and iPrefer loyalty programs.
places.history: The Ninth Avenue and 17th Street buildings were sold in 1987 to Covenant House, which ran them as a shelter for runaways; in 1994 the Chinese government acquired them and ran them as housing and services for Chinese artists, students and businessmen. In 2001 Sean K. MacPherson and Eric Goode bought the Ninth Avenue building for $19 million with the developers Richard Born and Ira Drukier. The adjacent 17th Street building was separately converted into the Dream Downtown Hotel in 2011, to designs by Frank Fusaro.
